module_title: Mughal Empire - Jagirdari Crisis, Decline, and Later Mughals
introduction: At this advanced level, we analyze the structural causes of the Mughal decline (such as the Jagirdari crisis), the impact of Aurangzeb's policies, the factionalism during the 'Later Mughals' period, and the accounts of European travelers who visited the empire.

core_concepts.title: The Jagirdari Crisis
core_concepts.description: According to historian Satish Chandra, during Aurangzeb's reign, the number of Mansabdars increased dramatically, but there was a shortage of fertile 'Jagirs' (land) to assign them. This 'Be-jagiri' led to intense exploitation of peasants and widespread agrarian revolts.

core_concepts.title: Aurangzeb's Deccan Policy
core_concepts.description: Aurangzeb spent the last 25 years of his life in South India fighting the Marathas, Bijapur, and Golconda. This exhausted the treasury and ruined the military. It is often termed the 'Deccan Ulcer' that ruined the empire.

core_concepts.title: Shifts in Religious Policy
core_concepts.description: Akbar abolished the 'Jizya' (tax on non-Muslims) in 1564. Aurangzeb re-imposed it in 1679, which alienated the Rajputs, Sikhs, and Marathas, eroding the empire's support base.

core_concepts.title: Accounts of Foreign Travelers
core_concepts.description: Englishmen Captain William Hawkins (1608) and Sir Thomas Roe (1615) visited Jahangir's court. French physician Francois Bernier visited during Shah Jahan/Aurangzeb's time and heavily critiqued the lack of private land ownership in India.

core_concepts.title: Nadir Shah's Invasion (1739)
core_concepts.description: During the reign of the weak Later Mughal 'Muhammad Shah Rangeela', the Persian ruler Nadir Shah defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal. He looted Delhi, taking the Kohinoor diamond and the Peacock Throne.

important_entities.name: Syed Brothers
important_entities.significance: During the Later Mughal period, they became so powerful that they enthroned and deposed several emperors at will (e.g., the assassination of Farrukhsiyar).

important_entities.name: Farrukhsiyar
important_entities.significance: In 1717, he issued a 'Farman' (often called the Magna Carta of the Company) granting the British East India Company duty-free trading rights (Dastak) in Bengal.

important_entities.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar (II)
important_entities.significance: He was the symbolic leader of the 1857 Revolt. The British exiled him to Rangoon (Myanmar), officially ending the Mughal Empire.

important_entities.name: Francois Bernier
important_entities.significance: Author of 'Travels in the Mughal Empire'. He argued that the crown's ownership of all land prevented economic progress and impoverished the peasantry.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Permission to Trade vs. Duty-Free Trade
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Jahangir granted the initial permission to the British to set up a factory at Surat. However, the special 'Farman' for duty-free trade (Dastak) in Bengal was given much later by Farrukhsiyar in 1717.
Students often assume Nadir Shah attacked immediately after the Great Mughals. Remember, his invasion (1739) happened 32 years after Aurangzeb's death, during the reign of Muhammad Shah.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar, Muhammad Shah Rangeela.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Qasim Brought, Akbar Stopped, Aurangzeb Reapplied, Rangeela Dropped
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Muhammad bin Qasim (Started), Akbar (Abolished), Aurangzeb (Re-imposed), Muhammad Shah Rangeela (Abolished completely).

exam_strategy_tips: For UPSC and State PCS exams, focus heavily on analytical (statement-based) questions regarding the 'Jagirdari Crisis' and the economic reasons for the Mughal decline.
Practice matching foreign travelers (Hawkins, Roe, Bernier, Tavernier, Manucci) with the specific Mughal emperors who were reigning during their visits.
